name: Ritsurin Garden
label: Ritsurin Garden
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/60252671: large area 'Ritsurin Garden' (784 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Historic Edo-period daimyo strolling garden at the foot of Mount Shiun.

text.description: Ritsurin Garden is a large, historic strolling garden in Takamatsu, laid out around ponds, little hills and winding paths, with the wooded slope of Mt. Shiun ("Purple Cloud Mountain") rising behind it. Work began in 1625 under the local feudal lord Ikoma Takatoshi, and successive lords kept improving it until it was completed in 1745. It opened to the public in 1875 and was named a Special Place of Scenic Beauty in 1953. The garden covers 750,000 square metres, so you will not see it all in one frame. The southern part is in the traditional Japanese style, with old teahouses and pine trees clipped into careful shapes. That is where phone photos tend to work best. Still water gives you reflections, the pines give strong shapes, and the mountain gives a calm green backdrop. The ponds also hold koi, which can add a bit of life to a close shot. Take your time and walk a little between pictures, because the view changes at almost every bend in the path. Keep the phone steady with both hands, and wait a moment for other visitors to move out of the shot.
text.geographic_location: Ritsurin Garden lies in Takamatsu, on the east side of Mt. Shiun, which forms its backdrop. It sits in a former river bed, so the mountain is always close by.
text.directions_text: No nearby station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a local map or the garden's official site for the best way to reach it. The phone icon on the map is about 30 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wide, natural view of pond, pines and mountain. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are close to a pavilion or a clipped pine and want to fit it all in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single pine, a teahouse roof or koi at the water's edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 30 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the water's edge on a lower line, with the trees and Mt. Shiun in the upper part of the frame. Keep the horizon level. Include a branch or a pine in the foreground to give a sense of depth. For a wider scene, try a slow panorama along the water, moving the phone smoothly.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main subject to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the greens and reflections stay rich. If you shoot koi, try a Live Photo, then choose the best frame afterwards. Wipe the lens before you start.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people, and a calm day gives the clearest reflections.

text.access_note: This is a major public garden that may have an entry fee and set opening times, so check the official site before you go.

name: Takamatsu Castle
label: Takamatsu Castle
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2381052708: the OpenStreetMap point 'Takamatsu Castle'.
notes: Seaside castle ruins with moat and sea bream in Tamamo Park.

text.description:
Takamatsu Castle sits right on the edge of the Seto Inland Sea, in front of Takamatsu port, and is now a public park. It is also known as Tamamo Castle, a name that refers to its moats, which are filled with seawater. Only three castles in Japan are known to use seawater moats, so the water is part of what makes this spot different. For a phone photo, the combination works well: dark stone walls, still water, pine-dotted banks and old wooden turrets all fit into one frame.

The castle was begun in 1588 by Ikoma Chikamasa and finished by 1590. The whole site covered about 400 by 200 metres. The main keep was taken down in 1884 because of its age, so you will not see a tall tower. Instead, look for the surviving Edo-period turrets and gate buildings, such as the Tsukimi Yagura and the Ushitora Yagura, which date from the late 1670s. The Sakuragomon gate, burned in the Second World War, was rebuilt in 2022. Also in the grounds is the Hiunkaku, a former Matsudaira family villa built in 1917.

Take your time and walk the paths beside the water, because the best angles change every few steps. Use the moat as a foreground and let the stonework lead the eye towards the turrets.
text.geographic_location: In central Takamatsu, Kagawa Prefecture, on the Shikoku island coast beside Takamatsu port. The castle is located on the coast of the Seto Inland Sea, in front of Takamatsu port.
text.directions_text: The castle is about a ten-minute walk from JR Shikoku Takamatsu Station. The phone icon on the map is about 75 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the walls, water and turrets together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the moat and want more stone and sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the roof tiles and the timber turrets.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 75 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Pause here first, then move a few steps along the path to try different angles on the water and walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the line of the moat edge on the lower third, with the turret or wall above it. Include some water in the foreground so the stone has a reflection or a sense of depth. Keep your phone level so the walls do not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is washing out. If the water is calm, wait for a still moment before you press the shutter.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone, and fewer harsh shadows than midday.

text.access_note: The castle grounds are a park, but entry arrangements and which areas are open can vary, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer on stone walls than midday light.
Calm water may give a clearer reflection of the walls and turrets.

name: Takamatsu Symbol Tower
label: Symbol Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Takamatsu Symbol Tower' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/250706903: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Symbol Tower' (102 m across).
notes: Tall glass tower in the Sunport waterfront district.

text.description:
Takamatsu Symbol Tower is a 30-storey skyscraper in Takamatsu, Kagawa Prefecture, finished in 2001 and standing 151 metres tall. What makes this spot work is the walkway on the west side. From there you can fit the tower, the lit trees around its base and a distant strip of sea into a single frame. A travel blogger calls it a favourite, and notes it is much quieter than the big-city sights in Tokyo or Osaka.

Because the tower is so tall, the main job is deciding how much of it to include. Stand back along the walkway and keep the whole building in the picture, with the trees in the foreground and the water behind. The phone icon on the map is right at the tower, so you do not need to hunt for a separate viewing place.

If you want a different angle, two alternatives are worth a look. The rooftop of the neighbouring Sunport Takamatsu building gives a lower view of the tower. Takamatsu Port is another viewpoint for the tower. Keep your phone lens clean, and have a quick look at the edges of the frame for lamp posts and signs before you tap the shutter.
text.geographic_location: In Takamatsu, beside the Sunport Takamatsu complex. The photo spot is the pedestrian walkway on the tower's west side.
text.directions_text: Use a map app on your phone to plan the route from where you are staying, searching for Takamatsu Symbol Tower or Sunport Takamatsu. Look for the tower itself, a 151-metre skyscraper. Once you reach it, walk to the pedestrian walkway on its west side, which is the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the tower, the lit trees and the sea together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and cannot fit the whole tower in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the top of the tower or to pick out the sea in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the tower is in the foreground, with the lit trees around it and the sea in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so it does not lean. Keep the trees low in the frame and let the sea sit as a thin band behind. Hold the phone level, as tilting it upwards makes the tower lean inwards. For a different view, try the rooftop of the neighbouring Sunport Takamatsu building for a lower angle, or Takamatsu Port for another view of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the lights do not wash out. If you shoot after dark, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or with both elbows tucked in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The lit trees are part of the view, so the lights should be visible after dark, but check locally for the lighting times if you plan around them. Daytime also works for a clear view of the tower and the sea.

text.access_note: The west side walkway is a public pedestrian walkway; for the building's observation deck or the Sunport rooftop, check the official site before you go.

name: Yashima-ji
label: Yashima-ji Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '屋島寺' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '屋島寺' (node/11757109024): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/422803840: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline '84 Yashima-ji' (248 m across).
notes: Shikoku pilgrimage temple No. 84 on top of Yashima.

text.description:
Yashima-ji sits on top of Yashima, a flat-topped lava plateau to the north-east of Takamatsu. It is the eighty-fourth temple on the Shikoku 88 temple pilgrimage, so you may see pilgrims in white among the other visitors. The temple is a Shingon temple and a branch of Ninna-ji in Kyoto. Tradition says it was founded by the monk Ganjin in 754 and later converted by Kōbō Daishi. Its tiled Hondō dates from 1618 and is an Important Cultural Property, as are a Heian-period wooden statue of Senjū Kannon and a temple bell from 1223. A museum holds temple treasures and items linked to the Battle of Yashima.

For photographs, the best subject is the vermilion main hall. Two stone tanuki statues guard its front, and the temple's gates frame the scene. The bright red paint, grey stone and surrounding trees give a phone camera plenty of colour and contrast to work with. Stand on the approach in the temple grounds, aim north towards the hall, and try to fit the hall, the tanuki and part of a gate into one frame. Then step in close for a second shot of a single tanuki with the hall blurred behind it. If you want the view over the city and the Seto Inland Sea, that comes from the lookouts on the mountain, such as Shishi no Reigan, and not from the temple grounds. Take the temple photos here and the view photos there.
text.geographic_location: Yashima-ji is on the Yashima plateau, in the north-east of Takamatsu in Kagawa Prefecture. It stands on the mountaintop, away from the city centre.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check your route to the Yashima summit before you go. Once you are on the summit, follow the signs to the temple. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the main hall and the tanuki together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the gates or the full width of the hall will not fit. Use telephoto (2x or more) for roof details and the faces of the statues.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in the temple grounds, from the approach in front of the vermilion main hall). The vermilion main hall of Yashima-ji with the two stone tanuki statues guarding its front, framed by the temple's gates. The exact position may vary, so move a few steps to find the best framing.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the hall on the upper-middle line, with a tanuki in the lower corner to give depth. Keep the phone level so the roof lines stay straight. If you want a different picture, the lookouts at Shishi no Reigan and Kenbokuen on the mountain show the city and sea, but the temple is not in those views.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red hall to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the vermilion stays rich and the sky does not wash out. Use portrait mode for a close shot of a tanuki.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kindest to the red paint, and early visits are often quieter. Dusk suits the lookouts better than the temple grounds.

text.access_note: This is an active temple on the Shikoku pilgrimage, so be respectful, check signs about photography inside the buildings, and check the official site before you go.

name: Ushitora Yagura
label: Ushitora Turret
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OSM N6632660605 (IMPORTANT CULTURAL PROPERTY TAKAMATSU-JO KYUHIGASHINOMARU(Takamatsu Castle Former Eastern Outworks) USHITORA-YAGURA(Ushitora Turret)): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Surviving castle turret, an Important Cultural Property.

text.description:
Ushitora Yagura is a turret, a small defensive tower, that belongs to the old Takamatsu Castle grounds. It is listed as an Important Cultural Property, as part of the castle's former eastern outworks. It is a good subject for a phone because it is a single, clear shape: pale walls and a tiled roof that stand out well against the sky and the trees around it.

Start with the default lens (1x) and fit the whole building in, with a little sky above the roof. Then switch to 2x or more to pick out the roof tiles, the wall texture and the windows. Turn on the gridlines and line the base of the walls up with a horizontal line, so the tower does not lean in the picture. If the sky is bright, tap the turret to focus and slide the exposure down a little, so the white walls keep their detail. Walk a few steps to either side for a second angle, perhaps with a branch or the castle wall framing one edge. Please check the official site before you go, as some parts of the castle grounds may be ticketed or have set opening times.
text.geographic_location: Ushitora Yagura stands in the old Takamatsu Castle grounds in Takamatsu, on the castle's former eastern side.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. The phone icon on the map is about 50 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the whole turret. Switch to telephoto (2x or more) for roof and wall details. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you stand very close and want to show the surrounding trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Take a few steps left or right to change the angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep the turret in the centre or on a third of the frame, with sky above and some greenery at the sides. Use the gridlines to keep the walls upright. Hold the phone level and avoid tilting it up, as this makes the tower lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the turret to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the white walls look too bright. Take a few shots so you can pick the sharpest.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Mid-morning to early afternoon in clear weather should give the south-facing side of the turret good light. Early morning is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: Access rules for the castle grounds and the turret may vary, so check the official site before you go.

name: Geishun Bridge
label: Geishun Bridge
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OSM W839555084 (Geishun Bridge): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Small bridge near Flying Monkey Rock in the garden's south.

text.description:
Geishun Bridge is a simple, quick stop on the Takamatsu map, and it suits a phone well because you can take the photo from very close by. Stand there and face east, and the bridge sits straight ahead of you.

Bridges are good subjects because they give a photo a clear structure: a line that leads the eye through the frame, with the surroundings behind it. Use that here. Put the bridge across the lower or middle part of the picture rather than dead centre, and let the space around it show where you are. Turn on the gridlines in your camera app and line the bridge up with one of the horizontal lines so it looks straight rather than tilted.

Take one wide shot to show the setting, then a closer one that fills the frame with the bridge itself. If anyone passes through the frame, wait a moment and take the shot when the scene is quiet, or let a passer-by give a sense of scale. Because you are so close, check the edges of the frame for bins, signs or parked vehicles, and take a step left or right to remove them.

I have no confirmed history, dimensions or dates for this bridge, so enjoy it for what you can see on the day.
text.geographic_location: Geishun Bridge is in Takamatsu. Use the map to see exactly what lies around the bridge, as I have no named district or landmark to give you.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed near this spot, so use the map to find your way to the bridge. The bridge is about 11 metres to the east, a few steps on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 10 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the bridge. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are standing close and cannot fit it all in. Try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot that leaves out distractions.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 10 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From here the bridge is straight ahead, so you can shoot it with almost no walking.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and set the bridge along a horizontal line so it sits level. Leave some space around it to show the setting. Take one wide frame, then a closer one. Move a step sideways to keep bins, signs and vehicles out of the picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge on the screen to focus, then slide your finger down on the exposure slider if the sky is washing out. Hold the phone steady with both hands and your elbows tucked in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight in the morning or late afternoon is usually kinder than harsh midday sun. After dark, try night mode and rest your elbows on something solid to keep the shot sharp.

text.access_note: Access details for this spot are not confirmed, so check local information before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Gridlines, tap-to-focus and the exposure slider are available on most smartphone cameras.
Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually more flattering than midday sun.
Night mode is available on many recent phones and works best with a steady hold.
Bins, signs or parked vehicles may appear near the bridge and spoil the frame.

name: Yashima
label: Yashima Plateau
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '獅子の霊厳' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '獅子の霊巌' (way/422803851): middle (7 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q3571905: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Flat-topped mesa and site of the famous 1185 battle, with a Seto Sea view.

text.description:
Yashima is a district and mountain in Takamatsu, with a summit observation deck overlooking the Seto Inland Sea and the city. The photo spot here is the terrace at 獅子の霊厳, on the western edge of the plateau. From there the sun sets over the water while the Takamatsu cityscape spreads out below, which gives you a classic sunset-to-night view. Guides name it as one of Japan's best sunset and night-view spots and the standard photo stop on Yashima.

The mountain also has some history. It is known for Yashima-ji, the 84th temple of the Shikoku 88 temple pilgrimage, and it was a decisive battleground in the Genpei War (1180–1185) between the Taira and Minamoto clans. A summit observation deck looks out over the sea and the city.

For photos, plan to arrive in the late afternoon. The last half hour of daylight and the period just after sunset are the best moments, because the sky colours and the first city lights appear in the same frame. If you have time, two other recommended viewpoints are worth a look. 遊鶴亭 gives a wide view of the sea and its islands with boats crossing, and 長崎の鼻 shows boats passing close below a small cape.
text.geographic_location: Yashima is a district of Takamatsu, in Kagawa. The terrace at 獅子の霊厳 is on the western edge of the mountain-top plateau, looking over the city and the Seto Inland Sea.
text.directions_text: A shuttle bus is reported to run from Kotoden Yashima Station to the top of Yashima, but check the timetable locally before you go. The terrace at 獅子の霊厳 is on the western edge of the plateau. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the sunset and the city below. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the coastline and sky, and try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out boats on the water or a stretch of the city.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 獅子の霊厳 (western edge of the plateau). The sun setting over the Seto Inland Sea with the Takamatsu cityscape below, the classic sunset-to-night view. If it is busy, the viewpoints at 遊鶴亭 or 長崎の鼻 offer a different view of the sea and islands.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line, depending on whether the sky or the city is the star. Keep a bit of foreground, such as the terrace edge, to give a sense of height. For a wider scene, try panorama mode and move slowly and evenly. For something different, walk to 長崎の鼻 and frame boats passing below the cape with the islands behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sunset colours are not washed out. After sunset, use night mode and rest your elbows on a wall or railing to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into dusk. Aim to be in place for the last half hour of daylight and stay for the period just after sunset.

text.access_note: The terrace is reported as freely accessible, but the rest of the mountain includes a temple and other facilities, so check the official site before you go.

name: Sunport Takamatsu
label: Sunport Takamatsu
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q7640975: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Waterfront promenade and ferry pier with a view over the Seto Inland Sea.

text.description:
Sunport Takamatsu is the redeveloped district beside the port, where Takamatsu's trains, ferries, buses and taxis all come together. It stands on the site of the former Takamatsu Freight Depot in Hamanochō. Today it holds a shopping mall, a hotel, apartments, convenience stores and several restaurants. It is also the passenger terminal for JR Shikoku's Takamatsu Station and for the ferries at the Port of Takamatsu, and JR Shikoku has its headquarters here. For a visitor, that makes it a good place to photograph a working modern harbour area rather than a single landmark.

It can work well on a phone if you step back as far as the surroundings allow, which may let you fit a whole frontage into the frame. Look for clean lines of buildings, the movement of people heading to ferries and trains, and any gaps that show the sky or the waterside. Because this is a busy transport hub, you will often have people walking through the scene. That can add life to a picture, but wait a moment if you want a cleaner view.

Take a first wide shot from there, then walk closer for details such as signs, entrances and reflections. Ritsurin Garden and Takamatsu Castle are the other well-known sights nearby if you want to continue your photo walk.
text.geographic_location: Sunport Takamatsu is in Hamanochō, on the Takamatsu waterfront next to the port and JR Takamatsu Station.
text.directions_text: Start from Takamatsu Station, since Sunport serves as its passenger terminal. If you are coming from elsewhere in the city, go by bus or taxi to the Sunport area in Hamanochō. The phone icon on the map is about 380 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the buildings and surroundings in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as signs or rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 380 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. Start with a wide view, then walk closer for details.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the edges of the buildings with them so the verticals stay straight. Keep the phone level and hold it at chest height rather than tilting it up, which stops the buildings leaning. Include a little foreground, such as paving or a railing, to give a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest building or sky area to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. If you shoot after dark, try night mode and rest your elbows against your body or a solid surface to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into the early evening is a good choice, when the light is softer and the building lights start to come on. Midday also works if you want clear, bright views, but expect more people about.

text.access_note: The district is a mix of public areas and shops, a hotel and transport facilities, so check the official site before you go for any restrictions inside particular buildings.

People are often walking through the area, as it is a busy transport hub.
Late afternoon and early evening give softer light, and building lights come on around dusk.
Takamatsu Station is the natural starting point for visitors arriving by train.
